description.summary: A 19th-century Brazilian cryptid reported chiefly in southern Brazil — described as a vast subterranean black-scaled worm or eel-like creature blamed for tunnels, trenches, and toppled trees — investigated by Auguste de Saint-Hilaire (1846) and Fritz Müller (1877–1878) and now generally treated as a folkloric explanation of soil-erosion and slumping events.
description.full: The Minhocão (Portuguese for 'big earthworm', augmentative of minhoca) is a Brazilian cryptid documented in 19th-century reports from the southern Brazilian provinces of Santa Catarina, Paraná, and São Paulo, with extension into northern Argentina and Uruguay. Witnesses described an enormous subterranean creature variously likened to an earthworm, eel, or serpent, with tough black scales, no clearly visible legs, and (in some accounts) a pig-like snout or paired tentacle-like appendages. Length estimates ranged from 20 to 80 m; widths from one to three metres. The creature was credited with tunnelling beneath houses and roads, gouging long trenches, undermining riverbanks, and dragging horses and cattle into the water. Two important 19th-century naturalists investigated: French botanist and explorer Augustin François César Prouvençal de Saint-Hilaire reported on the creature in December 1846 from accounts at Padre Aranda and Lake Feia in Goiás and elsewhere, and German-Brazilian zoologist Fritz Müller (a correspondent of Charles Darwin) published an article in the German journal Zoologischer Garten in 1877 drawing on accounts by Senhor Lebino of Curitibanos. Both proposed identification with a giant South American lungfish (Lepidosiren); later cryptozoologists (notably Bernard Heuvelmans) revived the case as a relict glyptodont or giant amphibian. Modern Brazilian commentators generally treat the Minhocão as a folk explanation for soil-piping erosion, slumping, riverbank collapse, and seismic activity in southern Brazil's heavy red earth.

etymology.origin: Portuguese; a regular augmentative of minhoca ('earthworm') with the suffix -ão.
etymology.first_use: Recorded in 19th-century Brazilian Portuguese; in scientific literature from Saint-Hilaire (1847) onward

related_phenomena.name: Mongolian Death Worm
related_phenomena.description: Other large subterranean cryptid reported far away

features.description: Reports give lengths of 20 to 80 m (60 to 240 ft); one 1878 account specifies '50 yards in length and 5 in breadth'
Witnesses describe a tough, armoured, black scaly hide
Francisco de Amaral Varella's account specifies a snout 'like a pig'
Some accounts describe a pair of tentacle-like growths near the head; earlier reports mention horns
The signature physical trace is large trenches, depressions, and toppled trees attributed to the creature's passage

physical.morphology: An enormous, elongate, mostly limbless subterranean creature; both Saint-Hilaire and Müller compared it morphologically with a giant lungfish.

abilities.description: Said to gouge long trenches and undermine riverbanks during heavy rain
Reportedly seizes horses and cattle from the bank and pulls them under
Witnesses report rumbling sounds, sometimes described as thunder, accompanying its movement; some claim these sounds 'presage a period of rainy weather'

patterns: Activity reported chiefly during and after heavy rain
Reports concentrate in southern Brazil (Santa Catarina, Paraná) and adjoining areas
Reports decline sharply after the late 19th century

range.description: Reports concentrate in southern Brazil (especially Santa Catarina and Paraná around Curitibanos), with secondary reports in Goiás and São Paulo; Saint-Hilaire's accounts also included locations such as Padre Aranda and Lake Feia.

hotspots.name: Curitibanos, Santa Catarina

location.description: Inland town of Santa Catarina, Brazil

hotspots.notes: Setting of Senhor Lebino's accounts collected by Fritz Müller and published in 1877

hotspots.name: Padre Aranda / Lake Feia

location.description: Padre Aranda and Lake Feia, Goiás, Brazil

hotspots.notes: Sites of accounts compiled by Saint-Hilaire in December 1846

first_recorded.source: Saint-Hilaire's December 1846 reports from Padre Aranda and Lake Feia

peak_activity_periods.description: Period of active reporting in southern Brazil and scientific investigation by Saint-Hilaire and Müller

origins.cultural_roots: 19th-century Brazilian rural folklore concentrated in southern Brazil's pampas and Atlantic-forest fringe.
origins.earliest_accounts: Saint-Hilaire's 1846 collections; published in 1847 in the Revue des Deux Mondes.
origins.folklore_connections: Sits within a broader Brazilian tradition of subterranean and water-creature folklore (Boitatá, Boiúna, Iara) and within the 19th-century European interest in 'living fossils' such as lungfish.

timeline.event: Saint-Hilaire collects Minhocão accounts at Padre Aranda and Lake Feia in Goiás
timeline.significance: Earliest scientific documentation of the creature

timeline.event: Saint-Hilaire publishes 'Le Minhocão' in the Revue des Deux Mondes
Fritz Müller publishes an article on the Minhocão in Zoologischer Garten, drawing on Senhor Lebino's accounts at Curitibanos and proposing a giant South American lungfish (Lepidosiren) identification
Müller is reported to have suggested he could obtain a Minhocão specimen for European collections; no specimen was ever produced
Bernard Heuvelmans's Sur la piste des bêtes ignorées (On the Track of Unknown Animals) revives the Minhocão case in cryptozoology
timeline.significance: Re-entry of the creature into 20th-century cryptozoological literature

history.modern_era: After the 1880s, reports tail off and the Minhocão is treated as a historical phenomenon. Modern Brazilian writers and geologists generally regard the case as a folkloric reading of soil-piping erosion, slumping, and earthquake-like events in heavy southern Brazilian soils, while a minority cryptozoological tradition keeps the dossier open.

notable.name: Saint-Hilaire's Goiás reports

location.description: Padre Aranda and Lake Feia (Lagoa Feia)

credibility_factors: Reported by a leading European naturalist

notable.description: Saint-Hilaire compiled local accounts in December 1846 of an enormous worm-like creature said to have drawn horses and horned cattle into the water at Padre Aranda and Lake Feia. He proposed identification with a giant lungfish.
evidence: Saint-Hilaire's 1847 Revue des Deux Mondes article
sources: Saint-Hilaire, A. (1847), Revue des Deux Mondes

notable.name: Müller / Senhor Lebino, Curitibanos

credibility_factors: Reported by Fritz Müller, an established correspondent of Charles Darwin

notable.description: Fritz Müller compiled second-hand accounts from Senhor Lebino at Curitibanos describing trenches and disturbed earth attributed to the Minhocão; he proposed identification with a giant South American lungfish.

credibility.notes: Most influential 19th-century report; central to the modern dossier.

notable.name: Francisco de Amaral Varella, southern Brazil

location.description: Southern Brazil (specific locality not preserved in the citation)

credibility_factors: Named witness recorded in contemporary accounts

notable.description: Francisco de Amaral Varella reported encountering a Minhocão approximately 50 yards long and 5 yards broad with armoured scales and a pig-like snout, in southern Brazil c. 1878.
evidence: Contemporary newspaper / journal coverage referenced in Wikipedia

credibility.notes: Cited in modern overviews via the Wikipedia summary.

trace.name: Trenches and toppled trees
trace.description: Long trenches, slumps, and lines of toppled trees attributed by 19th-century witnesses to the Minhocão's passage in southern Brazil.
trace.analysis: Modern geological reading attributes such features to soil-piping erosion, riverbank slumping, and seismic activity in heavy red soils, rather than to a biological agent.

documentary.name: Le Minhocão (Saint-Hilaire, 1847)
documentary.description: Article in the Revue des Deux Mondes presenting Saint-Hilaire's compiled accounts of the Minhocão.
documentary.analysis: Foundational European-language record of the creature.

documentary.name: Müller's Zoologischer Garten article (1877)
documentary.description: Article by Fritz Müller in the German journal Zoologischer Garten presenting accounts collected at Curitibanos and proposing a giant lungfish identification.
documentary.analysis: Most influential 19th-century scientific treatment of the Minhocão.

scientific.name: Giant South American lungfish (Lepidosiren)
scientific.description: Saint-Hilaire and Müller proposed that the Minhocão is an unusually large specimen — or relict population — of the South American lungfish (Lepidosiren paradoxa) or a related Ceratodus-like form, accounting for its eel-like body, swampy habitat, and burrowing behaviour.
evidence_cited: Eel-like body proportions in eyewitness reports
Lepidosiren is genuinely native to the region
Burrowing habit of lungfish during dry seasons

scientific.name: Surviving glyptodont or giant amphibian
scientific.description: Bernard Heuvelmans and later cryptozoologists suggested the creature might represent a relict glyptodont (giant armadillo-related Pleistocene mammal) or a giant caecilian-like amphibian.
evidence_cited: Pleistocene South American megafauna as comparable in size

skeptical.name: Geomorphological misreading
skeptical.description: Most modern Brazilian commentators treat Minhocão reports as a folkloric explanation of natural soil-piping erosion, riverbank slumping, and seismic events in heavy southern Brazilian soils, especially during heavy rains.
evidence_cited: Trench and slump features in southern Brazilian soils
Decline of reports as scientific geomorphology explained these features
Absence of any specimen, bone, or photograph in over a century

traditions: Southern Brazilian rural folklore, especially in Santa Catarina, Paraná, and Goiás
19th-century European 'living fossil' enthusiasm in which Minhocão reports were assimilated
stories: Saint-Hilaire's 1846 Goiás accounts (Padre Aranda, Lake Feia)
Müller / Senhor Lebino accounts at Curitibanos
Francisco de Amaral Varella's southern Brazil report
folklore.beliefs: By the late 20th century, the Minhocão was treated by Brazilian audiences chiefly as a historical curiosity and a piece of regional folklore.

literature: Le Minhocão — Augustin de Saint-Hilaire (Revue des Deux Mondes, 1847)
On the Track of Unknown Animals — Bernard Heuvelmans (1955; later eds.)
film_tv: Brazilian and international cryptozoology documentary segments
other: The 'Minhocão' elevated road in São Paulo (officially Elevado Presidente João Goulart) is named after the creature for its long, sinuous shape, but is unrelated to the cryptid
